title: 🥤 Soda streaming wars
body_text: Who’s for a game of six degrees of sartorial separation? Kevin Bacon, whose name lends itself to a game where people have to connect Hollywood figures back to the “Footloose” star in as few steps as possible, now hopes to be linked up with something much dearer to him: a box of clothes from the ‘90s. In a video posted to Instagram, the 68-year-old actor detailed the worldwide journey that the clothes have been on via New York, Memphis, France, Germany, Israel, and England, seemingly calling out FedEx as the offending courier behind the weeks-long route. Bacon sent out the plea with hopes to be reunited with the “old boots, old jeans, and old hats” in his original intended delivery destination of Ireland, and a spokesperson from the delivery giant has since confirmed they are now in direct contact with Bacon’s team. When you imagine the prolonged talks and tense negotiations that are thrashed out between some of the biggest names in global business, you might not imagine rooms of execs and franchisees sipping samples of innovative new tinctures, but that’s apparently how it went down in Texas over a couple of days in June , as KFC prepared to decide on a drink supplier moving forward. The choice, as it has often been for companies and customers alike through the years, was simple: Coke or Pepsi ? Follow in the footsteps of McDonald’s, Burger King, Wendy’s and many more by partnering with the most recognizable beverage brand of all time, or stick with Pepsi, the company that spun the chicken chain off as part of Yum! Brands in 1997 and has provided its drinks selection since the original acquisition some 40 years ago? This time, the Yum! fast-food behemoth went for Coca-Cola, switching from Pepsi in a move that mirrors the American soda-loving population at large. According to figures shared with Snacks by industry insights and analysis company Beverage Digest, Pepsi’s share of the carbonated soft drink market in the US has fallen from just over 13.6% at the start of the twenty-first century, to a little over 8% as of last year. In that time, Coca-Cola’s share has slipped much more slightly, down from 20.2% in 2000, to a still-strong 18.5% in 2025. In addition, last year was the third in a row where Dr. Pepper has taken a bigger share of the market than Pepsi, with Sprite and Diet Coke now also not far behind, taking 7.9% and 8% of soda case sales in the US, respectively. While it’s not the end of the world for Pepsi — the drinks giant will maintain its partnerships with international branches of KFC — it’s still a big blow, as Coca-Cola extends its already dominant position in the soft-drink fountain game, where it currently accounts for 70% of sales by volume, per separate Beverage Digest data . title: ❓Two Musk companies, one big question
body_text: Dyson wants to replicate the success of its vacuums and hair products but in your mouth. So far it is not going so well. The company’s $500 Camerajet toothbrush (powered by AI, of course) sprayed water across the bathroom and then stopped working, according to one Bloomberg reporter who tested the product . It was also incredibly hard to find stocked in any major retailer, they reported. Stocks ended a rocky week down on Friday. Elon Musk has found another way for his two companies to collaborate, leaving some wondering whether a more formal union could be next. On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the long-awaited second-generation Tesla Roadster, a sports car developed with the help of his rocket company SpaceX . During a demonstration in Texas, the vehicle drove upside down, flipped through the air, and jumped over a row of other Teslas using rocket-style thrusters powered by compressed air. The company says the Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than a second, reach speeds exceeding 230 mph, and travel more than 300 miles on a single charge. “You’re going to see some crazy stuff tonight,” said Musk, who is CEO of both companies. “You’re going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.” Deliveries for the long-delayed vehicle aren't expected until 2028. (The second gen Roadster was first announced by Musk in 2017 with delivery slated for 2020. Tesla's reservation agreement explicitly says the company cannot guarantee when the Roadster will be delivered or whether it will be delivered at all.) Musk also said he was "not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions." It will almost certainly spark some sort of regulatory review from the Federal Aviation Administration, Wired points out . But the Roadster's biggest significance may have less to do with its ability to fly than with the company helping it get off the ground. The unveiling has added fuel to speculation that Musk could eventually combine Tesla and SpaceX, bringing his electric-car business and rocket company under one roof. Prediction market traders increased the odds of a merger being announced by early next year. One Barclays analyst predicted that such a merger could happen before the end of this year. The Roadster is unlikely to do much for Tesla's bottom line. Musk has previously described the Roadster as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially." Tesla reports earnings this week, with analysts penciling in $19.6 billion in quarterly automotive sales, a 7.5% decline from the same period last year. As Tesla's traditional car business faces pressure, Musk is increasingly pitching investors on a future built around AI and robotics — areas where his companies' ambitions overlap. Veteran tech analyst Gene Munster put it best in an X post : “Two takeaways from tonight’s Roadster event. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. Elon can’t wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together.” The cumulative market capitalization for quantum computing companies IonQ , D-Wave , and Rigetti is virtually unchanged from where it was in early September 2025, right before those companies ramped in part on speculation over US government support. The fundamentals of the industry at large really haven’t meaningfully improved over the past year, nor have they deteriorated. And quantum computing is not a space where most traders were looking for hockey-stick growth now, it’s more about the prospect for technological breakthroughs that have the potential to spur parabolic operational improvements further down the road. The key underlying factor may be that the speculative energy just is not there anymore for this part of the market. Major pure-play quantum computing companies that have been around for a few years (like IonQ, D-Wave, and Rigetti) have seen call volumes drop precipitously from their 2025 peaks. While there are some nascent signs of potential risk-defined falling-knife-catching in some of these names via options lately, it’s nothing to write home about yet. — Luke Kawa, read the rest in EntryPoint Go deeper with EntryPoint . title: 🥊 Core bob and weave
body_text: It’s a boom time for Advent calendars, with wholesale sales of the countdown-to-Christmas products up 63% year over year. The holiday tradition, where kids can get perhaps a chocolate or a small toy each day in the season of Advent ahead of the big day, has wound up at the confluence of a couple of major toy-industry trends . What is an Advent calendar if not 24 blind boxes you get to crack open? Is the thrill not the same as that of opening up a trading card pack or a video game lootbox? And with adults now buying most of the toys for themselves, anyway, what could play better to a “kidult” audience than an ostensibly religious way to give yourself toys for a whole month? Coreweave had a wild week, with anxieties about its debt spurred by a rather candid comment by one of its founders — and stoked by Elon Musk — spiraling into a broader moment of anxiety around just how much money the AI revolution is requiring investors to put up. A full-court press from CoreWeave’s boosters appeared to reset expectations , but where does this all leave us as we assess the state of the AI trade? CoreWeave shares sold off as much as 15% on Wednesday after a remark from a cofounder about the company’s attempts to get an investment-grade rating that would allow it to borrow from insurers rattled markets, with the executive describing the capital as “unlimited, like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche.” That put a bit of a spotlight on the company’s debt situation, as the 2031 CoreWeave bonds yield 15%, which is very very high for a company in its position. Well, amid the renewed scrutiny the cost of protecting that debt against default for five years rose to 1,194 basis points , 74.5 basis points in a day, swaps pricing in a 60% chance of default within five years. Wow , one might think, even Elon Musk is worried about the AI bubble? No. No he is not. Don’t be ridiculous. Elon Musk simply owns a competitor: SpaceX is rapidly attempting to build out large AI data centers that can both reduce its reliance on — and ultimately compete with — neoclouds like CoreWeave. In fact, as Grok and the other products of SpaceX’s AI lab continue to lag rival products out of Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet , Meta and so on, the core shareholder value of SpaceX’s AI business will be the neocloud element that can eventually sell compute to those winning teams. Remember, SpaceX cut a $1 billion a month deal to sell compute in September, which of course leads to the question of “why does SpaceX have excess compute?” Elon’s “yikes” is, if anything, more kicking a rival when they’re down rather than any concession that the technology he has tied his fortune to has issues. So, where does that leave us? Well, CoreWeave stock finished up 5% Thursday, still down 17% over the five-day, with its CEO waving the week away saying “there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” The unique cultures of Silicon Valley and Wall Street have been in general alignment that the AI boom is going to make a lot of people a lot of money. But before we get cocky, it’s worth remembering two axioms held as truth in either camp that apply very well : From the West coast: the future is already here — it's just not very evenly distributed. From the East coast: markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent. The AI boom’s benefits to shareholders will not necessarily be evenly distributed. If, for instance, there are one or two models that get a lot of pickup or achieve milestones faster than rivals can achieve, even companies that get lots of money in investment will not be worth a whole lot. If the world runs all its AI out of data centers, the neoclouds win; if, on the other hand, we don’t need all these buildings and you can eventually run a solid model on a phone, then the neoclouds will bite it. Heck, maybe free Chinese open source models can do 97% of the work of AI, and the American labs become boutique R&D firms arguing with academics over whether they actually solved theoretical math problems. In short: There are lots of worlds in which both LLMs are popular, useful technologies integrated into the American economy, and also some of the companies getting high valuations don’t exist anymore. Sure, which companies win and which companies lose that future could be decided by breakthroughs in AI model development or a phalanx of Nvidia chips powered by fusion power or a data center deployed to space, or any of these big and exciting reasons that a company might win that investors like to imagine. But for lots of them, their victory or their death will be decided by the rather boring parts of the balance sheet describing how much money they owe creditors in 2032. Whether this week was actually the axis upon which the AI trade turns is a bit premature. But it is the shape of things to come, a taste of what the future will at some point bring, at least when everyone flips their cards on the table and the winnings get divided. Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it. Just ask Character.ai .
